newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German Q1 GDP data leaves goals hard to reach.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German Q1 GDP data leaves goals hard to reach.

text.p: Germany's economy grew only 1.4 percent in the first quarter, the government said on Thursday, raising more questions over whether Bonn can qualify for the single European currency despite adjusted figures showing higher growth.
When corrected for calendar factors, gross domestic product (GDP) grew a more encouraging 2.8 percent from the same quarter last year, the Federal Statistics Office said.
But the figures cast doubt on whether the government could reach its target of 2.5 percent growth this year.

They suggested little relief for Germany's towering unemployment rate, the cost of which is a major problem as Bonn desperately tries to cut its budget deficit to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Most private sector economists appeared to accept the higher of the growth figures as giving a more accurate picture of the economy. But they still took it with a grain of salt and said Bonn would have a hard time reaching its target of 2.5 percent growth for the full year.
"The calendar factors won't necessarily be made up in the rest of the year," said economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt.

An early Easter meant there were three fewer workdays in the first quarter this year than last year, shaving more than a full percentage point off the economic growth rate, the Statistics Office said.
German hopes of qualifying for EMU ride on the GDP goal as sluggish growth and continued high unemployment hamper efforts to trim the budget deficit to target levels.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has repeatedly said Germany will be able to meet its EMU goals, but bases that forecast on the economy growing 2.5 percent.
"The latest indicators are more positive, but unfortunately they are not yet impacting on the labour market...The data could be positive for the deficit," said Waigel.

But private observers were sceptical. "The economic expansion is too weak to change the situation on the labour market," analysts at Trinkaus Capital Management said in a research note. "This year's budget deficit should exceed the crucial level of 3.0 percent of GDP."
Countries wanting to join EMU are supposed to cut their budget deficit to three percent of GDP.

German unemployment data for May, due for release on Friday, are expected to show a fall of only 90,000 to 4.25 million before seasonal adjustment. Adjusted figures are likely to show a higher rate for the month, analysts said.
Public consumption showed a surprising surge in the first quarter, perhaps because government agencies accelerated spending on expectations of a freeze on outlays later in the year.
Otherwise, private consumption remained lacklustre, and exports remained the main engine of growth.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said more lively capital investment was needed to improve the outlook for jobs and growth. But despite favourable conditions such as higher profits and low interest rates, corporations remain reluctant to invest in Germany.
Industrial orders data for April added an encouraging note, however, showing a 3.3 percent jump from March, and some economists were upbeat.
"Growth for the rest of the year may surprise on the upside," said Sonja Gibbs at Nomura International in London.
"Depending on the composition of GDP, we could see a little bit stronger growth than the markets have been anticipating, which could be good for the tax revenue position in Germany," she said.
First quarter GDP was up 0.4 percent from the previous quarter, when growth was 0.1 percent quarter-on-quarter, and 2.2 percent year-on-year, according to the Bundesbank.
Data from the central bank showed west German GDP grew 2.8 percent and east German GDP expanded 4.4 percent year-on-year, after calendar and seasonal adjustment.
